adaptation: Night-time comfort copy shows why awake-at-night moments are a strong opening for a Fajr story: the viewer is already awake, and the gap is what they do next instead of scrolling.
A one-line hope image proves a short visual line can carry a reminder; for Salah Alarm the lesson is to keep the hook short and put the waking mechanism, not more motivation, in the middle slides.
A direct verse warning works because it names forgetting plainly; for Salah Alarm it maps to the morning version of forgetting, where the phone comes first and prayer slips.
A comfort verse is useful for restart content: it lowers the shame of a missed week, which is exactly the audience a streak-based Fajr alarm needs to re-engage.
One Arabic word as the whole message shows minimal typography can outperform a paragraph; for Salah Alarm a one-word Fajr hook can carry a carousel that then explains the prayer-mat scan.
Friday framing plus everyday kindness shows occasion content can still point at personal consistency; for Salah Alarm the bridge is keeping a promise to yourself at Fajr, not only to others.
A superlative curiosity hook (shortest and strongest) earns the swipe; for Salah Alarm it reframes the Fajr problem as waking, not praying, since the prayer itself is short.
